Benchmarking Single-Shot Detector Scaling and Quantization Trade-offs for Real-Time Vehicle Collision Anticipation under Simulated Edge Hardware Constraints

CS 493: Scientific Communication — Assignment #01 Technical Report
Authors: Nishat Ahmad (2023574), Muhammad Riyan Javed (2023494)
Course: CS 493 (Scientific Communication)
Target Scope: Gap A (Severe Inference Latency Bottlenecks in Scaled Edge Detectors)
Date: November 15, 2026
Hardware Profile: Simulated 4 CPU Cores, 4GB RAM, POSIX cgroups / Physical CPU Affinity
Dataset: TU-DAT Road Traffic Anomaly Benchmark (10 Positive Crash + 5 Control Clips)

1. Executive Summary & Formal Problem Statement

Modern roadside Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) and edge Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) demand sub-second trajectory forecasting and vehicle collision anticipation to dispatch Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) pre-crash advisories before physical impact occurs. However, roadside edge compute nodes operate under strict thermal, power, and cost constraints (typically limited to 4 CPU cores, 4GB RAM, and no discrete GPU). While architectural scaling from Nano to Small improves spatial feature representation, deeper neural networks suffer catastrophic latency degradation on embedded CPUs, collapsing framerates below the essential 20–30 FPS real-time threshold (≤ 33.3–50.0 ms/frame).

This investigation rigorously evaluates YOLOv11 model scaling (Nano: 2.6M parameters vs. Small: 9.4M parameters) across three numerical precisions (FP32, FP16, and INT8 post-training quantization) paired with a 7-state SORT Kalman tracker and a kinematic Time-to-Collision (TTC) forecaster. The pipeline was comprehensively evaluated across 10 real-world collision sequences and 5 negative control sequences from the TU-DAT benchmark.

2. Core Research Questions Answered for Gap A

Question 1: Did INT8 Nano achieve the 20–30 FPS real-time threshold?
Empirical Finding: No. Across the 10-sequence multi-video evaluation, yolo11n_int8 achieved an average throughput of 17.71 ± 2.23 FPS (57.44 ± 7.75 ms). Under strict 4-core physical CPU affinity pinning, throughput dropped to 15.99 FPS (62.53 ms). Both fall short of the mandatory 20 FPS threshold.
Architectural Root Cause: While INT8 quantization compressed weight storage by 59.5% (10.64 MB → 4.31 MB), general-purpose edge CPUs without dedicated Vector Neural Network Instructions (VNNI) or AVX-512 INT8 GEMM hardware pipelines must emulate 8-bit arithmetic via software dequantize-compute-quantize cycles. This software emulation overhead completely negates memory savings, making INT8 Nano 38% slower than FP16 (26.08 FPS) and FP32 (24.03 FPS).
Question 2: How severe was the latency penalty of uncompressed Small (~7 FPS)?
Empirical Finding: Catastrophic (> 3.0× to 4.4× throughput collapse). Uncompressed Small (yolo11s_fp32) collapsed to 9.67 ± 2.76 FPS with a mean inference latency of 109.13 ± 20.43 ms/frame (p95: 126.59 ms). Under hard 4-core CPU affinity, yolo11s_fp32 yielded 9.64 FPS (103.77 ms) and yolo11s_int8 collapsed to 6.50 FPS (153.81 ms).
Physical Safety Hazard: At 109.1 ms/frame, a vehicle traveling at an urban speed of 60 km/h (16.67 m/s) advances 1.82 meters blind between frames (2.11 meters at p95 latency), severely truncating the reaction window and leading to late collision alarms.
Question 3: What is the Pareto-optimal configuration recommendation for roadside edge ITS?
Recommendation: yolo11n_fp16 is the decisively optimal configuration.
yolo11n_fp16 comfortably clears the real-time threshold at 31.18 ± 0.31 FPS (26.08 FPS under hard 4-core affinity, 38.35 ms latency), delivers a pre-crash warning margin of RTM = 1.69 ± 2.42 seconds before impact, maintains a verified 0.0% False Positive Rate on normal traffic, and halves model weight storage (5.33 MB vs 10.64 MB).

3. End-to-End System Architecture & Pipeline

The complete edge collision anticipation pipeline processes incoming roadside camera footage sequentially through four tightly integrated stages:

[Video Input Stream] (640x640 @ 30 FPS / 60 FPS) │ ▼ [Single-Shot ONNX Detector] ── YOLOv11 Nano / Small across FP32, FP16, INT8 │ ▼ (Bounding Boxes: [x1, y1, x2, y2, confidence, class]) [SORT Multi-Object Tracker] ── 7-State Kalman Filter (x = [u, v, s, r, u', v', s']^T) + Hungarian IoU Matching │ ▼ (Active Track Trajectories with Smooth Positions & Velocities) [Kinematic TTC Forecaster] ── Relative Velocity, Closing Speed (v_c), Closest Point of Approach (d_min) │ ▼ [Collision Advisory Engine] ── Trigger sustained alert iff: TTC < 2.5s, d_min ≤ R_coll, v ≥ 30 px/s, k ≥ 3 frames

3.1 Mathematical Formulations

1. SORT Multi-Object Kalman Filter: Each vehicle track state is parameterized by a 7D state vector:

x = [u, v, s, r, u', v', s']T

where (u, v) denotes 2D bounding box center coordinates, s = w × h is scale, r = w / h is aspect ratio, and (u', v', s') are their first-order temporal derivatives. Measurement vector z = [u, v, s, r]T updates the state covariance via the discrete Kalman gain equation.

2. Kinematic Time-to-Collision (TTC) & Lateral Closest Point of Approach (CPA): For any active pair of tracks i and j with center positions p_i, p_j and velocities v_i, v_j:

d = p_j - p_i,    v_rel = v_i - v_j,    v_c = (d · v_rel) / (||d|| + 10-6)
t_cpa = (d · v_rel) / (||v_rel||2 + 10-6),    d_min = ||d - v_rel · t_cpa||

A collision alert is triggered if and only if: (1) closing speed v_c > 0, (2) TTC = ||d|| / v_c < 2.5s, (3) lateral miss distance clearance d_min ≤ R_coll = (w_i + h_i + w_j + h_j) / 8, (4) dynamic vehicle velocity ≥ 30 px/s, sustained over k ≥ 3 consecutive frames. This formulation eliminated 100% of false alarms from opposite-lane traffic and parked vehicles.

3. Trajectory Coordinate Jitter Variance: High-frequency spatial instability introduced by model quantization is quantified via discrete acceleration variance across tracks:

Jitter = (1 / (N - 2)) ∑ || c_{t+1} - 2c_t + c_{t-1} ||2

4. Resolution Time Margin (RTM): Pre-crash alert warning horizon before ground-truth impact frame F_accident:

RTM = max(0, F_accident - F_first_alert) / FPS_video

5. Code Architecture & Modular Implementation Walkthrough

The repository is engineered into clean, production-grade, modular Python components:

  • models/export_onnx.py: Automates static-shape ONNX export for YOLOv11n and YOLOv11s. Sets input shape to [1, 3, 640, 640], applies OPSET 17, and produces FP32 and FP16 graph definitions.
  • models/quantize_int8.py: Implements Post-Training Static Quantization via ONNX Runtime QuantizeLinear / DequantizeLinear (QDQ) operators. Uses an ImageCalibrationDataReader calibrated on 144 diverse roadside traffic frames from TU-DAT. Explicitly protects all 84 regression conv, DFL, and detection head nodes (model.23) in full-precision FP32, preventing spatial mAP collapse.
  • tracking/kalman_tracker.py: Standalone implementation of the SORT algorithm. Implements a 7-state continuous Kalman filter with constant-velocity motion model, state prediction, measurement correction, and Hungarian bipartite matching over an IoU cost matrix.
  • tracking/collision_kinematics.py: Trajectory forecasting engine. Calculates relative displacement, relative velocity, line-of-sight closing speed v_c, Time-to-Collision (TTC), Closest Point of Approach (t_cpa), and minimum lateral miss distance (d_min). Enforces min_moving_speed = 30.0 px/s and inradius threshold to guarantee 0.0% false alarms.
  • data/dataset_loader.py: High-performance data pipeline for TU-DAT video clips and annotations. Optimizes sequential frame decoding via OpenCV, eliminating repetitive CAP_PROP_POS_FRAMES seeks to reduce per-frame I/O decode overhead from ~90ms to 4.4ms (a 20× speedup).
  • benchmark/runner.py: Multi-video benchmarking engine. Enforces simulated edge CPU constraints (4 worker threads, sequential scheduling, and optional OS-level CPU affinity pinning). Runs all 6 configurations across 10 positive collision videos and 5 negative control clips, outputting consolidated CSV/JSON metrics.
  • benchmark/metrics.py: Mathematical implementation of mean/p95 latency, detection mAP@50, trajectory coordinate jitter variance, and Resolution Time Margin (RTM).
  • analysis/pareto_plotter.py: High-DPI publication visualization generator. Computes Pareto non-dominated sets and exports publication-ready 300 DPI figures with error bars and zone shading.
  • docker/run_benchmark.sh & run_benchmark.ps1: Containerized benchmark runners executing under POSIX control groups (--cpus="4.0" --memory="4g").
  • tests/test_pipeline.py: 9 comprehensive pytest verification tests covering Kalman lifecycle, TTC convergence/divergence, lateral filtering, dataset discovery, and metric calculation.

6. Final Academic Conclusions for CS 493

  1. Validation of Gap A: Architectural scaling from YOLOv11-Nano to YOLOv11-Small induces a severe latency penalty ($109.13 ext{--}127.82\, ext{ms/frame}$ vs. $23.73 ext{--}32.08\, ext{ms/frame}$), reducing throughput to single digits ($6.5 ext{--}9.7\, ext{FPS}$) and leading to dangerous vehicular blind travel distances ($> 2\, ext{meters}$). Scaled detectors cannot be deployed on edge CPUs without dedicated hardware ASICs.
  2. The INT8 CPU Emulation Paradox: Without specialized VNNI/AVX-512 hardware support, INT8 quantization incurs software quant/dequant emulation penalties that make INT8 Nano ($15.99 ext{--}17.71\, ext{FPS}$) slower than FP16 ($26.08 ext{--}31.18\, ext{FPS}$), dropping it below the 20 FPS threshold.
  3. Definitive Recommendation: yolo11n_fp16 is the Pareto-optimal configuration for roadside edge ITS, delivering real-time throughput ($26.08 ext{--}31.18\, ext{FPS}$), a pre-crash warning horizon of $1.69\, ext{seconds}$, 0.0% false alarms, and a 50% model storage footprint reduction.
